## Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will:

- Understand what genomics is and its applications in breeding
- Know the difference between genotype and phenotype
- Learn about molecular markers used in breeding
- Be familiar with common genomic data formats

## What is Genomics?

**Genomics** is the study of genomes - the complete set of DNA within a single cell of an organism. In breeding, genomics helps us:

1. Identify genes associated with desirable traits
2. Predict breeding values more accurately
3. Accelerate breeding cycles
4. Improve selection efficiency

### :::{.callout-note}
**Key Concept:** While genetics studies individual genes, genomics looks at all genes and their interactions simultaneously.
:::

## Genotype vs Phenotype

Understanding the difference is crucial:

| Term | Definition | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Genotype** | Genetic makeup of an organism | DNA sequence at a specific locus |
| **Phenotype** | Observable characteristics | Plant height, yield, disease resistance |

The relationship can be expressed as:

$$ \text{Phenotype} = \text{Genotype} + \text{Environment} + (\text{G} \times \text{E}) $$

## Molecular Markers

Molecular markers are DNA sequences with known locations on chromosomes. Common types include:

### SNP (Single Nucleotide Polymorphism)

The most common marker type in modern genomics:

```r
# Example SNP data structure
snp_data <- data.frame(
  marker_id = c("rs12345", "rs67890", "rs11111"),
  chromosome = c(1, 1, 2),
  position = c(10583, 10611, 17324),
  ref_allele = c("A", "G", "T"),
  alt_allele = c("G", "A", "C"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(snp_data)
```

### SSR (Simple Sequence Repeats)

Also known as microsatellites:

```r
# Example SSR data
ssr_data <- data.frame(
  marker = c("RM1", "RM2", "RM3"),
  motif = c("(GA)n", "(CT)n", "(AT)n"),
  size_range = c("100-200 bp", "150-250 bp", "80-180 bp"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(ssr_data)
```

## Common Data Formats

### VCF (Variant Call Format)

Standard format for storing genetic variation:

```
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##FORMAT=<ID=GT,Number=1,Type=String,Description="Genotype">
#CHROM  POS     ID      REF     ALT     QUAL    FILTER  INFO    FORMAT  Sample1 Sample2
1       10583   rs12345 A       G       .       PASS    .       GT      0/0     0/1
1       10611   rs67890 G       A       .       PASS    .       GT      0/1     1/1
```

### PED/MAP Format

Common in PLINK for genome-wide data:

```r
# Reading PLINK format data (using snpStats package)

```

## R Packages for Genomics

Essential packages to install:

```r
# Install Bioconductor (if not already installed)
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# Core genomics packages
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "data.table", "ggplot2"))

# Bioconductor packages
BiocManager::install(c(
  "SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP144.GRCh37",  # Human SNP data
  "BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19",        # Human genome
  "VariantAnnotation",                   # VCF handling
  "genio"                                # PLINK file I/O
))

# Breeding-specific packages
install.packages(c(
  "rrBLUP",      # Ridge regression BLUP
  "BGLR",        # Bayesian regression
  "sommer",      # Mixed models
  "qtl",         # QTL mapping
  "qtl2"         # Next-gen QTL mapping
))
```

## Loading Genomic Data

Example workflow with SNP data:

```r
# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(rrBLUP)

# Simulate example genotype data
set.seed(123)
n_markers <- 1000
n_individuals <- 200

# Create genotype matrix (0, 1, 2 for AA, Aa, aa)
genotype_matrix <- matrix(
  sample(0:2, n_markers * n_individuals, replace = TRUE),
  nrow = n_individuals,
  ncol = n_markers
)

# Add individual IDs and marker names
rownames(genotype_matrix) <- paste0("Ind", 1:n_individuals)
colnames(genotype_matrix) <- paste0("M", 1:n_markers)

# Check data structure
dim(genotype_matrix)
head(genotype_matrix[, 1:5])

# Check allele frequencies
allele_freq <- colMeans(genotype_matrix) / 2
hist(allele_freq, 
     main = "Allele Frequency Distribution",
     xlab = "Frequency",
     col = "steelblue",
     border = "white")
```

## Quality Control Basics

Before analysis, always check data quality:

```r
# Function to check missing data
check_missing <- function(genotype_data) {
  missing_per_ind <- rowSums(is.na(genotype_data)) / ncol(genotype_data) * 100
  missing_per_marker <- colSums(is.na(genotype_data)) / nrow(genotype_data) * 100
  
  list(
    individuals = missing_per_ind,
    markers = missing_per_marker
  )
}

# Apply QC check
qc_results <- check_missing(genotype_matrix)

# Plot missing data
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(qc_results$individuals, 
     main = "Missing Data per Individual",
     xlab = "% Missing",
     col = "lightblue")
hist(qc_results$markers, 
     main = "Missing Data per Marker",
     xlab = "% Missing",
     col = "lightgreen")
```

### :::{.callout-warning}
**Important:** Always perform quality control before genomic analysis! Common filters:
- Missing data < 10%
- Minor allele frequency (MAF) > 0.05
- Remove individuals with high missing data
:::
